items.title: Protecting Democratic Process from Manipulation in last 48-72 Hrs by Opaque Algorithmic Virality
items.abstract: This paper identifies and addresses a structural vulnerability in AI-driven platforms: the ability to distort public perception in the final 48–72 hours before a critical decision point without any visible rule violation. In modern digital ecosystems, content alone is no longer the primary source of harm. The greater risk lies in the scale, speed, and precision of algorithmic amplification, which can transform otherwise ordinary content into systemic influence. Put simply: in 2018, harm could often be understood as content; in 2026, harm is increasingly content multiplied by massive amplification at scale, especially within narrow and highly consequential time windows. At the center of this paper is a dual risk vector: narrow decision windows and last-stage amplification. I examine how contemporary amplification systems can be exploited by external actors to distort public discourse, influence market sentiment, and manufacture artificial consensus without formally breaching platform rules or easily triggering detection systems. By combining AI-generated content with coordinated engagement strategies, adversaries may manipulate visibility, perceived agreement, and narrative dominance during sensitive periods such as regulatory consultations, public health emergencies, product launches, IPO windows, or policy debates. In decision environments that are already finely balanced, even a marginal change in perceived sentiment may be enough to alter the apparent majority. A shift in the visible views of only 2–3% of active participants can become highly consequential when institutions, regulators, investors, or citizens are making judgments under time pressure. Repetition and disproportionate visibility can shape how people interpret events, particularly those who are undecided or still forming their views. In such contexts, amplification itself becomes the instrument of influence. The risk becomes especially acute in the final 48 hours before a key deadline or public decision. At that stage, heavily repeated narratives can move faster than oversight. Regulators, fact-checkers, journalists, and review bodies often do not have sufficient time to verify, contextualize, or respond before perceptions harden and decisions are made. In effect, last-minute amplification can shape outcomes before meaningful scrutiny becomes possible. My analysis argues that current defenses remain structurally inadequate because they are largely reactive and content-focused, while the real locus of influence lies in the mechanics of amplification. Existing approaches are designed mainly to identify problematic content after dissemination, leaving a critical enforcement gap at the point where visibility, reach, and momentum are actually created. This paper therefore not only identifies the structural risk but also proposes a response that works without changing existing laws such as the DSA, GDPR, or AI Act. Through a technical framework based on WTO GATS-compatible algorithm-level verification, it advances control at the point of execution, before amplification occurs. The objective is to enable deterministic enforcement of compliant algorithmic behaviour rather than relying solely on post hoc detection. In doing so, the paper shifts the governance focus from reacting to harm after it scales to preventing it at the stage where systemic influence is actually produced. 1. Scenario Overview Consider a regulatory consultation, a corporate shareholder decision, or a public health debate where the outcome is shaped by perceived public sentiment — often reflecting only a narrow margin of expressed opinion. In such environments: minor shifts in perception can alter outcomes; information exposure plays a decisive role; and digital platforms act as primary channels of public influence. To understand the risk, I ask the reader to conceptualise the platform's recommendation system as a "loudspeaker in a town square": it determines which messages are repeated; which voices are amplified; and which viewpoints remain unheard. Unlike traditional media, however, this loudspeaker is automated, opaque, and continuously adaptive. 2. Mechanism of Influence 2.1 No System Breach Required External actors do not need to hack or compromise platform infrastructure. Instead, they exploit normal system behaviour: Generate large volumes of content (including AI-generated text, images, or videos); Coordinate initial engagement (likes, shares, timing); Trigger algorithmic ranking systems; Allow platform algorithms to amplify the content organically. 2.2 Role of AI Artificial intelligence significantly lowers the barrier to entry for influence operations: High-quality synthetic content, including deepfake videos, can be generated at scale; Narratives can be tailored to specific demographics and behavioural profiles; Multiple content variants can be produced rapidly to evade detection systems; AI transforms influence operations from high-cost, manual campaigns to low-cost, automated and scalable amplification strategies. From Limited Coordination to Systemic Automation Even five years ago, such influence operations could not be executed at the same level of scale, speed, and coordination. Campaigns required significant human effort, manual content creation, and limited ability to synchronise activity across platforms. As a result, manipulation efforts were slower, less consistent, and easier to detect. Today, AI enables near-real-time generation of large volumes of content, synchronised activity across multiple channels, and continuous adaptation to platform behaviour and user response. This shift marks a transition from isolated or loosely coordinated actions to highly coordinated, system-level influence operations, making the current risk fundamentally different and significantly more severe. Mass Automation and Artificial Environment Creation Beyond content generation, AI enables large-scale orchestration of communication channels, allowing actors to simulate widespread public activity. This includes repeated circulation of synthetic or manipulated videos across multiple accounts, automated robocalls delivering consistent or targeted narratives, mass messaging campaigns across digital platforms, and auto-generated comments, replies, and engagement signals on posts. When executed in coordination, these activities create an artificial information environment in which certain narratives appear dominant or widely accepted, users perceive high levels of support or urgency, and algorithmic systems interpret engagement as organic popularity. Amplification Feedback Loop These artificial signals are then reinforced by platform algorithms: Stage 1: Synthetic content is introduced into the ecosystem. Stage 2: Automated engagement signals (likes, shares, comments) are coordinated around the content. Stage 3: Algorithmic amplification is triggered — platform systems interpret the engagement as organic popularity. Stage 4: Increased visibility follows, as the content is surfaced to progressively larger audiences. Stage 5: Perceived legitimacy is established — users interpret high visibility as evidence of genuine public support. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle where fabricated activity drives real visibility, and real visibility further legitimises the fabricated narrative. Irreversibility of Impact A critical challenge arises from the speed and scale of this process. By the time manipulation is identified, content may have already reached large audiences, perceptions may have been formed or altered, and narratives may have been internalised by decision-makers and the public. Even if the content is later removed or labelled, the impact is often irreversible, particularly in time-sensitive contexts such as regulatory deadlines or market-moving events. Key Insight: AI does not merely create misleading content; it enables the simulation of collective behaviour at scale. This shifts the risk from isolated misinformation to systemic perception manipulation, where the primary driver of influence is not the content itself, but the artificially constructed environment in which it is consumed. 2.3 Amplification vs Content Itself A single deepfake video, in isolation, has limited impact. A fake video cannot cause significant harm if it is not amplified. The real risk emerges when the same content is repeatedly surfaced, it reaches large audiences in a short time, and it is perceived as widely shared or endorsed. Harm ≠ Content | Harm = Content × Amplification Without exponential amplification, most manipulated content remains marginal, its influence is contained, and its detection and correction are manageable. With amplification, the same content becomes a narrative, perception shifts rapidly, and correction becomes ineffective. 2.4 Perception Formation Once amplification begins, content appears repeatedly across user feeds, perceived popularity increases, and users infer: "This must be important — everyone is talking about it." This creates a false consensus effect, where visibility is mistaken for legitimacy. 3. Amplification Risk in Narrow-Margin Decision Environments In contexts where outcomes are closely contested — whether regulatory consultations, shareholder votes, public health advisories, or policy debates — the margin between competing positions is often extremely narrow. items.title: Protocol-Dependent Ranking Inversion in Complementary Synthetic Cognitive Profiles
items.abstract: This technical note presents a minimal synthetic stress test on the legitimacy of global cognitive ranking under admissible protocol variation. Two synthetic cognitive agents with complementary performance profiles are evaluated across three task families: local-immediate, distributed-integrative, and mixed. A family of admissible evaluation protocols is then defined by varying the relative emphasis assigned to these task families while preserving their joint presence within the evaluative architecture. The central result is protocol-dependent ranking inversion: one agent ranks higher under protocols privileging locally segmentable performance, while the other ranks higher under protocols privileging distributed integration. A balanced global score can still produce an apparently unified ranking, but that ranking is shown to depend partly on the evaluative interface rather than on a protocol-independent dominance relation between the two profiles. Although the note is fully synthetic, the same diagnostic issue is directly relevant to LLM benchmark systems, where global rankings are often derived from heterogeneous task families and aggregation protocols. The note does not argue against evaluation in general and does not address human psychometrics directly. Its aim is narrower: to show, in a controlled synthetic setting, that a global score may partly rank interface compatibility rather than cognitive organization alone.

items.title: Protostage-NET: A Clinically Guided Foundation Model With Prototypical Learning for Automated Amd Grading From Oct Images
items.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss, where accurate staging is essential for treatment. However, most recent approaches for OCT images remain limited to binary classification and do not capture the full clinical spectrum of the disease. To address this gap, we propose ProtoStage-Net, an explainable foundation model framework for fine-grained AMD staging. Our method leverages the DINOv2 vision foundation model as a backbone, fully fine-tuned for OCT data, and introduces two clinically inspired attention mechanisms: the Clinically Guided Channel Attention (CGCA) module, which emphasizes diseaserelevant feature channels, and the Lesion Localization Module (LLM), which highlights pathological retinal regions. Classification is performed through a hierarchical prototypical learning strategy at binary, ternary, and detailed six-class levels, providing transparent similarity-based decisions. In addition, we incorporate temporal ordinal constraints to enforce clinically valid AMD progression pathways. We evaluate ProtoStage-Net on a cohort of 954 OCT B-scans acquired from three different imaging devices. Our framework achieves a macro F1-score of 93.49 %, surpassing the baseline foundation model by more than 2 % and outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the clinical explainability of our approach, with saliency maps confirming that ProtoStage-Net accurately localizes lesion regions across different AMD grades.

items.title: Quantifying the relationship between physical environmental variables and interruption events during the medication process: An observational study
items.abstract: Interruptions during medication administration threaten patient safety in ICUs, yet their relationship to physical environmental features remains poorly understood. This observational study examined interruptions and recorded travel paths across three ICUs by shadowing 18 nurses during 100 medication rounds (29.25 h). Data were initially analyzed using descriptive statistics, path visualization, and heatmaps. Multiple linear regression was applied to examine relationships between layout variables and interruption number and duration. A total of 1,115 interruptions were recorded, primarily self-initiated (21.97%) and nurse-to-nurse interactions (18.30%). Travel distance strongly predicted interruptions, with each 100-foot increase causing a 26.8% increase. Medium and large units had 45% and 43% fewer interruptions than small units. Noon rounds had 31.6% fewer interruptions than afternoon rounds. Interruptions lasted longer at nurse stations (31.28-54.50s) and corridors (33.81-51.56s) than in patient rooms (26.48-43.57s). Results indicate that travel distance and unit size significantly impact interruption patterns, suggesting evidence-based design strategies can optimize ICU environments and improve medication administration safety.

items.title: Quantization of Artificial Intelligence Models for Personal Protective Equipment Detection in Industrial Environments
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the quantization of an artificial intelligence (AI) model designed to detect personal protective equipment (PPE) in industrial settings. The base model is developed using YOLOv8, which achieves an accuracy rate exceeding 80%. Quantization is applied to optimize the model by converting floating-point values to integers, thereby reducing computational complexity. The performance of the quantized model is validated on Jetson Nano, an embedded hardware platform capable of detecting protective gear for workers across various scenarios.
